Closing three loops on an AKM11E servo

Custom nested FOC servo control on a bare metal STM32F411 + DRV8353RS gate driver, designed using system identification and frequency domain controller design.

01

Background

Project purpose

Develop and validate a single axis embedded servo controller representative of an industrial precision motion application.

Background

This project grew out of a conversation with a former coworker at a wafer dicing company. Their team is considering developing an in house motion controller for a machine incorporating an XYθ stage and coordinated laser galvo control. This FOC servo controller is a single axis proof of concept designed around that use case. The original performance targets followed common industrial servo practice: a 20kHz current control update rate and approximately 500Hz current loop bandwidth.

Project phases

  1. Hardware bring up: connect the motor, encoder, gate driver, and Raspberry Pi 5. Develop the embedded firmware, then run the control algorithms against a simulated motor plant before applying them to real hardware.
  2. Motor characterization: with the motor unloaded, identify its electrical and mechanical dynamics, design the current, velocity, and position controllers, and verify their performance against measured hardware data.
  3. Stage integration: connect the motor to a ball screw stage, characterize the additional inertia, friction, compliance, and backlash, and redesign and validate the controllers for the complete mechanical system.
  4. Motion execution: implement a trapezoidal trajectory generator on the STM32, driven by Pi issued motion commands over SPI, and verify tracking performance of the validated cascade against a real move.

Development began at the innermost loop and progressed outward: current, velocity, and then position. For each loop, the results show the measured or modeled plant, the controller designed against it, and the measured closed loop response. Loop gain crossover frequency and phase margin are evaluated for each loop as well, backed out from the closed loop measurement.

The current loop runs at 20kHz. Each outer loop targets 60° of phase margin and a bandwidth at least three to five times lower than the loop beneath it.

The current loop targets 250Hz bandwidth, verified at 2.07V/A, 2450V/(A·s). This was kept conservative due to suspected shunt current sense noise at higher gain, and has not been revisited since.

All plant measurements were obtained from frequency response sweeps performed on the hardware, and the captured data was analyzed offline in Python.

Current loop. The motor's electrical transfer function was initially calculated from its datasheet resistance and inductance, then checked against a measured frequency response. A PI controller was designed using pole zero cancellation with a target bandwidth of 250Hz. The loop gain response was evaluated for crossover frequency and phase margin, and a closed loop sweep was performed to verify the achieved bandwidth and current tracking.

Velocity loop. The velocity plant was measured with the current loop closed underneath it. A direct open loop iq to velocity sweep became unusable below about 10.5Hz (large excursions; true dynamic instability not confirmed) for reasons not fully understood; back EMF was suspected but doesn't fully fit, since measured velocity stayed low, and friction was considered but should be light on this unloaded motor. A workaround was found regardless: closing a light proportional velocity loop first stabilized this, and the underlying plant was backed out algebraically from its known controller and measured closed loop response. A PI velocity controller was then designed using pole zero cancellation, targeting a 50Hz bandwidth. The completed loop was swept again, independently, to verify its real closed loop response.

Position loop. The position loop plant combines the measured closed loop velocity response with the integration from velocity to position. Because the plant already contains an integrator, a proportional controller is sufficient to set the position loop bandwidth. The loop gain was evaluated for crossover frequency and phase margin. A closed loop frequency sweep and position step test were then used to verify bandwidth, tracking accuracy, overshoot, and settling behavior.

02

Hardware & firmware architecture

Everything below runs on hardware and firmware built from scratch for this project: an STM32F411 driving a TI DRV8353RS gate driver, with a Raspberry Pi 5 that logs telemetry and runs the offline analysis. No vendor motor control SDK: the ISR structure, PWM/ADC synchronization, and all three control loops are custom, not provided by a vendor framework.

Actuation & sensing (STM32F411)

TIM1 center aligned PWM (CMS=01) at 20kHz drives the DRV8353's three half bridges. Phase currents come back through an ADC1 injected conversion group, hardware triggered off the same PWM timer and serviced in an ISR, so current sampling is phase locked to the switching edge, not free running. Rotor position is an incremental quadrature encoder read entirely in hardware by TIM2's encoder mode counter (both edges, 32-bit, no software pulse counting), signal conditioned through a line receiver.

Control & comms

Three nested loops share the 20kHz ISR: current every tick, velocity every 4th (5kHz), position every 20th (1kHz). The DRV8353 gate driver is configured and monitored over SPI1. A second SPI peripheral streams fixed format telemetry frames to the Raspberry Pi 5 under Pi generated clocking, which does all offline system ID and Bode analysis in Python (Welch/CSD cross spectral estimation, nonlinear least squares fits). Nothing below runs on device.

Current loop: open loop plant identification

A voltage chirp on vq drives the motor while iq is measured. Welch/CSD cross spectral estimation gives the transfer function directly; a first order model P(s) = 1/(Ls+R) is fit to the coherent band by nonlinear least squares.

The fitted model tracks the measured points almost exactly; the nominal datasheet derived curve (R=1.55Ω, L=1.02mH, halved from line to line specs) sits close but isn't what any gain below is actually designed against. Every Kp/Ki here uses the fitted values.

04

Current loop: controller design

The PI zero is placed at the plant pole (Ki/Kp = R/L), converting the open loop dynamics to a pure integrator by construction. Kp then sets the crossover directly. Note the plant fit above is only coherent to 150Hz, but this design targets a 250Hz crossover: above 150Hz the first order model is an extrapolation, not a direct measurement, which is exactly why section 5's closed loop chirp exists as the primary check near the actual operating band.

05

Current loop: closed loop verification

To verify the controller design, a chirp sweeps iq,cmd with the current PI closed around it, measuring the closed loop response H(s) = iq,meas / iq,cmd directly and comparing its achieved bandwidth against the 250Hz design target.

DC gain

Closed loop response: H(s) = iq,meas / iq,cmd, measured
measured, coherence ≥0.8 coherence 0.5 to 0.8 single pole curve fit

Measured bandwidth (300Hz) runs above the 259.9Hz analytical prediction from section 4's ideal pole zero cancellation. One unconfirmed lead: the deployed Ki/Kp (1183.6/s) is placed against the CSD fitted R/L (1162.4/s, only 1.8% off), so the zero cancellation matches the fitted plant, not the datasheet. But swapping in the datasheet's nominal inductance (1.02mH vs. the fitted 1.275mH) into gc=Kp/(2πL) predicts 323Hz, much closer to both measured numbers than the fitted-plant prediction. That's a real correlation, not a confirmed mechanism: it would mean the fitted inductance overstates whatever governs the closed loop response near 300Hz, for reasons not yet checked.

06

Velocity loop: plant identification

A direct open loop sweep here became unusable below about 10.5Hz (large excursions; true dynamic instability not confirmed). Root cause not fully understood: back EMF was suspected, but measured velocity stayed low, which doesn't fit that explanation; friction was also considered, but should be light on this unloaded motor. A workaround was found regardless: the mechanical plant is instead identified by closing a light P only velocity loop first, then backing out the open loop response algebraically using H = L/(1+L) ⇒ L = H/(1−H) ⇒ P(s) = L(s)/Kp, the same identity used for the current loop, extended one step since C(s)=Kp is a real constant for a P only controller.

07

Velocity loop: closed loop verification

Zero cancellation PI, sized against the plant identified above: Ki/Kp = 1/τ cancels the plant's pole, leaving a pure integrator loop, with Kp then sized for the 50Hz target crossover from step 06: Kp = 2π·fc,target·τ/K = 0.0205. An ideal integrator loop has 90° phase margin everywhere and gc = BW exactly; real discretization delay eats some of that margin, which is what closing the loop and measuring it directly is good engineering discipline for.

Position loop: verification

The outer loop is pure P, wrapped around the velocity loop above. No plant to fit here, since position integrates velocity by definition, so Kp is sized directly against the velocity loop's own verified closed loop data: target the position crossover at BW/4 of the velocity loop's measured bandwidth (80.4Hz), reading the actual measured gain there rather than assuming unity.

Phase 2

Motor Only Servo Drive Conclusion

The cascade behaves well: ~1% overshoot into a 2% settling band in ~36ms. The current loop runs at its 250Hz target gain, confirmed sufficient rather than assumed: pushing it to 500Hz and 1000Hz live on hardware left every outer loop's measured margin unchanged, while introducing real risk (audible noise, one genuine instability event) for no benefit, so the proven 250Hz target gain stays. The real ceiling on outer loop bandwidth is the backlash modulated mechanical resonance found near 65 to 90Hz, not current loop speed.

09

Phase 3: friction, feedforward, and re closing the loops

The motor is now driving a real linear stage (150mm travel, 2mm lead/rev) instead of spinning free. Friction was a problem: the same closed velocity loop chirp, run at two different command amplitudes (8 vs 15 rad/s), backed out plant gain/time constant numbers that differed by nearly 2x - a supposedly linear measurement that depended on signal amplitude. This section is that investigation, the fix, and the redesigned position loop verified against it.

9.1: Friction characterization

Closed velocity loop (real PI, not open loop) holding a series of constant velocities, 1 to 23 rad/s, both directions, repeated across 2 runs. Steady state iq at each hold is a direct measurement of the torque needed to overcome friction at that speed, not inferred indirectly.

9.3: New position loop, design and verification

With a confirmed linear system to design against, re derived Kp,pos with the same phase margin method as Section 8 (target crossover, gain sized off the measured response there, not assumed unity), giving Kp,pos=205.5. Closed loop verification measured only 39° PM against the 60° target, so the gain was backed off to Kp,pos=100 and re verified.

Real result, not textbook clean: the bode plot above shows something that looks like a resonance: a magnitude peak with phase collapsing 120°+ in a ~2.5Hz band right around 31Hz. Before treating that as a hardware problem, reran the chirp with only the velocity loop closed (same motor, same stage, no outer position loop) across the same band:
Velocity loop only, same hardware, same band: no resonance
measured, coherence ≥0.8

Clean, coherence 0.98+, no bump anywhere. Since the plant itself showed nothing there, the peak is the position loop's own closed loop peaking at its measured crossover (31.8Hz), the expected consequence of the reduced 39° phase margin, not the stage resonating. This is what motivated backing the gain off to Kp,pos=100 above.

Phase 3

Load Compensated Servo Drive Conclusion

Working position loop with every number measured against the loaded system: friction curve, feedforward, re verified linearity, closed loop margin, step response, and a resonance looking artifact traced back to loop margin instead of hardware. The first gain (205.5) came in short of the 60° margin target at 39° and was backed off to 100, restoring 70.6° PM.

Shunt current sense noise, flagged as the next step after Phase 2, was measured directly: ~130mA std at zero commanded current, about 30x the ADC's own quantization noise. A controlled test isolated one real contributor: the oscilloscope probe's ground clip injecting noise through a ground loop. Removing it cut the floor to ~85 to 95mA std. The remaining noise is still open.

10

Motion execution: real trajectory tracking

Past sysid characterization into an actual production move: the friction feedforward and corrected velocity gains ported onto a separate on STM trajectory planner branch (trapezoidal generator, real MoveCmd over SPI, not a sysid test harness), then executed a 10mm move with full position/velocity/following error telemetry.

Full trapezoidal move: commanded/measured position, following error, velocity

During constant velocity motion, the proportional position loop produces the finite ramp following error expected from a type-1 servo. With Kp,pos=205.5 s-1 and approximately unity velocity loop DC gain, the predicted following error is v/Kp: 48.7µm at 10mm/s and 4.87µm at 1mm/s. The measured values, 54.7µm (held steady through nearly the entire cruise, 99th percentile 53.5µm, not a transient spike) and ~5.0µm, closely match the model. Velocity feedforward is the natural next step for reducing this error without increasing position loop gain.

Phase 4

Motion Execution Conclusion

The validated cascade drives a real production style move correctly: following error matches the type-1 servo model almost exactly. Nothing here required new tuning; it is a verification of what Sections 3 through 9 already built.

11

Open items

  • Shunt current sense noise caps current loop bandwidth; not the active constraint today (mechanical resonance is), but would become the next one if that's fixed.
  • Open loop velocity sweep became unusable below 10.5Hz (large excursions); true dynamic instability not confirmed, root cause not understood.
  • Remaining shunt noise floor (~85 to 95mA std) unexplained. Meaningful reduction here would likely benefit the whole project.
  • Position loop steady state error (Ess=v/Kp, ~55µm at 10mm/s) should be fixed with velocity feedforward, not an added integrator (would cost margin this loop doesn't have).
  • Current loop measured bandwidth (300Hz) runs above the 250Hz target/259.9Hz prediction; root cause not isolated. Margin stays healthy (83.3°).
  • Position loop step response and bode chart in Section 9.3 still show the old Kp,pos=205.5 capture; pending re capture at the new Kp,pos=100.
